summary:
Brandenburg stands under the national framework of Germany: federal constitutional and equality protections apply nationwide, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove the federal floor. The Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 January 2025, allows adults to change their gender entry by self-declaration, and the same act sits behind Marla-Svenja Liebich's registration as a woman at the end of 2024.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Lands have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities.

Screening is a documented flashpoint at the border. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Reporting machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

In Cottbus on 20 October 2025, a rubbish container was set alight against the façade of the 'Regenbogenkombinat' queer cultural centre during CSD week; the fire was out in about fifteen minutes and nobody was hurt, but state security (Staatsschutz) took over the arson investigation and a political motive cannot be excluded. Local initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the attack sits among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city.

The subsequent Cottbus CSD, the 17th edition, under the motto 'Vereint in Frieden und Vielfalt', ran on 26 October 2025 with a large police deployment against two registered counter-demonstrations from the far right, one of them organised independently of the other. Police protection of the march and the security conditions around it are the operative facts for a visitor deciding whether to attend.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between written rule and applied practice is the recurring pattern across the sources. Section 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act permits identity-congruent placement only in exceptional cases, while the Liebich transfer in July 2026 shows a Land-level authority overriding a legal gender recognition on safety grounds and drawing an abuse-of-law objection from critics. A visitor should expect the outcome to depend on the receiving facility rather than on the document.

Reform is proceeding Land by Land rather than nationally. Rhineland-Palatinate added a § 17 to its prison act on 1 March 2026, and the Lower Saxony criminological institute is simultaneously researching trans prisoners, which indicates the model remains under construction and that a prison in Brandenburg may be operating under older, binary language.

Facility access beyond prisons has produced the same argument in civilian settings. The Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline of January 2025 turned a private association's rule into a national debate over women-protected spaces, and venues now apply their own reading of registered gender, so a trans woman's entry depends on the individual operator rather than on a single standard.

Hostility in Brandenburg is not hypothetical. The arson at the Regenbogenkombinat in Cottbus was referred to state security and is placed by local initiatives among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the same city, and the following CSD required a large police deployment against two registered counter-demos. The pattern resembles the security posture seen at Pride events elsewhere in Germany, where the risk sits with the demonstration rather than with the visitor's own conduct.
localsOnly:
German residents obtain gender recognition through the self-declaration route of the Self-Determination Act, and the resulting registry entry is what prison authorities, venues and employers must in principle read; residents can challenge a contrary placement through the Equal Treatment Act, as BASHKKA did with her airport complaint in June 2025.

Residents held in custody have a named point of contact in the Berlin prison service's German-language page for trans, inter and non-binary detainees, and the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony runs an ongoing research project on transgender prisoners that can be cited in advocacy.

Counselling and hate-crime support for residents is organised through the STOP the HATE site of the Prevention and Empowerment organisation, which maintains a topic-sorted counselling finder, an LSBTIQ* crisis line for emergencies, and guidance on preserving evidence and reporting to police.

Resident advocacy shaped the facilities debate: trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued publicly against claims that self-declaration would be invoked on a whim, and Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel documented how Berlin saunas and similar venues treat trans women after months of argument.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no Brandenburg-specific prison service instruction on housing trans detainees is sourced, so whether identity-congruent placement is offered in Brandenburg facilities at all is not established by this inventory.

Unresolved: the Staatsschutz investigation into the 20 October 2025 fire at the Regenbogenkombinat has no stated outcome or suspect in the sourced material, and the political motive remains explicitly unconfirmed.

Unresolved: the counter-demonstrations at the 26 October 2025 Cottbus CSD are reported as registered, but their size, any conditions attached to their route, and whether they made contact with marchers are not sourced.

Unresolved: no result is available for BASHKKA's June 2025 complaint under the Equal Treatment Act, and the airport's response to her statement is not documented here.

Unresolved: whether the Berlin prison service's guidance for trans detainees is mirrored by a Brandenburg prison service equivalent is not sourced; the reporting available is regional press coverage from Cottbus and the surrounding Lausitz area, which carries no information on custody, documents or entry screening in the Land.
